name: Philippians
author: The apostle Paul wrote this letter, with his younger co-worker Timothy named alongside him. Paul was a Jewish teacher from Tarsus, trained as a Pharisee (a group devoted to strict keeping of God's law), who once persecuted Christians before becoming a follower of Jesus and a travelling missionary who planted churches around the Mediterranean. He wrote while a prisoner awaiting trial. Traditionally this was in Rome around AD 60–62, though some scholars suggest an earlier imprisonment in Ephesus (mid-50s) or Caesarea.
audience: The letter went to the church in Philippi, a city in Macedonia (northern Greece), which Paul had founded around AD 49–50; its first members included a businesswoman named Lydia and a local jailer. It was a small, mostly non-Jewish congregation that faced opposition from outsiders and had generously supported Paul, recently sending him a gift by a messenger named Epaphroditus.
era: The Roman Empire ruled the Mediterranean world, with Nero as emperor at the likely time of writing. Philippi was a Roman colony, resettled with retired army veterans after a famous battle there in 42 BC, and its people were proud of their Roman citizenship and customs. Honouring the emperor was part of civic life, and a group that worshipped another Lord could draw suspicion. Prisoners like Paul often relied on friends to bring food and support while they waited, sometimes for years, for their cases to be heard.

notes.1:1: Paul greets the church's leaders, called overseers, and its deacons, helpers who served practical needs, an early glimpse of how local churches were organised.
notes.1:12: Paul reports that his imprisonment had become known among the guard, possibly the emperor's elite Praetorian Guard, while other preachers, some rivals, spoke freely.
notes.1:19: Paul writes while awaiting a court verdict that could mean either release or execution.
notes.2:19: Timothy, from Lystra in modern Turkey, had travelled with Paul for years and helped found the Philippian church; Paul planned to send him there.
notes.2:25: Epaphroditus was the Philippians' own messenger who brought their gift; he fell gravely ill, nearly died, and Paul was now sending him home.
notes.3:1: Paul warns against teachers who insisted non-Jewish believers be circumcised and keep Jewish law, and recounts his own background as a Pharisee from the tribe of Benjamin.
notes.4:10: Paul thanks the Philippians for the gift Epaphroditus brought, recalling that they alone had supported him earlier, including while he was in Thessalonica.
notes.4:21: Greetings come from believers in the emperor's household, meaning slaves and freed servants working in imperial service rather than the emperor's family.

flags.problem: The note states the opponents' identity as settled fact. Scholars disagree about who Paul is warning against here. The most common view is Christian teachers urging circumcision on non-Jewish believers, but some think he means non-Christian Jews or another group.
flags.suggestion: Hedge slightly, e.g. 'Paul warns against opponents, most likely teachers who insisted non-Jewish believers be circumcised and keep Jewish law, ...'
